paragraphs: Your local, firefighter-owned team. Care for the landscape you love.
Ornamental plant care · South Louisiana
Spotted leaves, sticky foliage, or a shrub that keeps declining? Grow Green looks at the plant, the symptoms, and the growing conditions to recommend treatment or the right next step.
Free estimate request · Clear recommendations · Local office follow-up
Start with what you can see
These are clues we review, not a diagnosis. Choose the closest match to add it to your request. We’ll look at the plant and the full pattern of symptoms.
Honeydew from insects such as aphids, soft scales, or whiteflies can support sooty mold. We look for the source of the sticky residue.
Tiny pale specks, bronzing, or fine webbing can be clues to mite feeding. Leaf undersides and active pests help clarify the cause.
Missing leaf tissue calls for a closer look at feeding activity and the damage pattern. The insect may be gone by the time damage is noticed.
Spots, blotches, or a powdery coating can point to disease. Plant identity and the pattern of symptoms help determine the next step.
We consider watering, drainage, roots, and nutrition along with pests and disease. Yellow leaves alone do not identify the problem.
Tell us whether one branch, one plant, or several plants are affected. That pattern helps guide a closer review of the plant and its surroundings.
Learn more about these clues: UC IPM on sooty mold · University of Minnesota Extension on spider mites · Extension guidance on tree leaf spots .
A closer look. A clearer plan.
We review accessible ornamental trees and shrubs, including landscape plants such as azaleas, hollies, camellias, and gardenias. Plant identity, size, access, and condition shape the recommendation.
Tell us when the problem started, how many plants are affected, and what has changed. Photos can help us plan the review.
We look for pest activity and disease signs while considering roots, moisture, and the planting site. Some concerns need a closer inspection or testing.
When treatment is appropriate, we explain the approach, price, and any follow-up. A watering change, further evaluation, or referral may also be part of the recommendation.
Serving Greater Baton Rouge, Ascension, Livingston, and nearby South Louisiana communities. Enter your property address so we can confirm coverage.
Free, no-obligation estimate
Request a free estimate for ornamental pest or disease care. Our office usually follows up within one business day, Monday–Friday, to review the concern and next steps. Fields marked * are required.
Choose an address suggestion or enter your details manually.
Use the city or community shown on the property’s mailing address.
No payment required to request an estimate. Your service address helps us confirm coverage and plan the next step.
Have photos? Keep them handy. Our team can help you share them when we follow up. Office hours: Monday–Friday, 8:00 AM–4:00 PM.

Thanks for reaching out to Grow Green. Our team will review your plant concerns and contact you about the next steps. Have any photos ready to share when we follow up. This request does not schedule a treatment.
Helpful details for your request
A few clear photos and a short history help us understand what is happening around the affected plants.
Show where the damage sits and whether nearby plants look different.
Capture affected leaves, their undersides, and any visible insects or coatings.
Include mulch depth, wet areas, irrigation, and the planting location.
Note recent planting, pruning, watering changes, or products already applied.
Have photos ready when our team follows up. We’ll help you share them with your request.
Care that fits your landscape
The next step depends on the problem and the plants. We can discuss targeted care and an ongoing program when each makes sense.
Start here when a tree or shrub is showing damage, pest activity, or unexplained decline.
Explore our separate six-visit program for seasonal monitoring and appropriate ornamental plant care throughout the year.
Pricing reflects the plants, their size and accessibility, the concern, and the recommended follow-up. We confirm the plan before you approve service.
Before we take a closer look
What to expect from assessment, treatment recommendations, and follow-up.

We review problems affecting eligible ornamental trees and shrubs, including plants such as azaleas, hollies, camellias, gardenias, and similar landscape plantings. Plant size, access, species, and the suspected problem help determine whether our service is appropriate.

Photos are a useful starting point. We may need to examine the plant and growing conditions in person, and some problems require a sample or laboratory testing. A photo of one damaged leaf may not reveal the full cause.

No. Watering, drainage, root injury, planting depth, sunlight, weather, and nutrient issues can produce similar symptoms. We consider those conditions before recommending an insecticide, fungicide, or nutritional treatment.

Existing holes and dead leaf tissue do not repair themselves. Appropriate treatment may reduce further damage and help protect new growth. Recovery depends on the cause, remaining plant health, and growing conditions; severely declined plants may need another solution.

Yes. Describe the current concern in the form. We review the property and explain whether targeted treatment, follow-up visits, a recurring program, or a different next step makes sense. Scope and pricing are discussed before you approve service.

This page helps you request care for an ornamental pest, disease, or decline concern. Our separate Tree & Shrub Care program provides six scheduled visits across the year for seasonal monitoring and appropriate plant-health care. We can discuss that option if ongoing support fits your landscape.

Pricing depends on the number, size, type, and accessibility of the plants, the problem being addressed, and the recommended follow-up. We confirm the service scope and price before you approve. A request through this page does not book an application.

Yes. Tell us when symptoms started and share recent planting, irrigation, pruning, weather, fertilizer, or pesticide changes. Include product names and application dates if you know them. This history helps us evaluate the concern and plan appropriate care.
Keep people and pets away from the treatment area during application. Follow the re-entry directions provided for the specific products used. The waiting period can vary by treatment.

Pruning, removal, stump work, and structural tree-risk assessment are outside this ornamental treatment service. A dead, storm-damaged, leaning, or otherwise unsafe tree should be evaluated by an appropriately qualified tree professional.

    Which plants can you help with?

    We review problems affecting eligible ornamental trees and shrubs, including plants such as azaleas, hollies, camellias, gardenias, and similar landscape plantings. Plant size, access, species, and the suspected problem help determine whether our service is appropriate.

    Can you identify the problem from a photo?

    Photos are a useful starting point. We may need to examine the plant and growing conditions in person, and some problems require a sample or laboratory testing. A photo of one damaged leaf may not reveal the full cause.

    Is every yellow or brown plant a pest or disease problem?

    No. Watering, drainage, root injury, planting depth, sunlight, weather, and nutrient issues can produce similar symptoms. We consider those conditions before recommending an insecticide, fungicide, or nutritional treatment.

    Will damaged leaves turn healthy again after treatment?

    Existing holes and dead leaf tissue do not repair themselves. Appropriate treatment may reduce further damage and help protect new growth. Recovery depends on the cause, remaining plant health, and growing conditions; severely declined plants may need another solution.

    Can I request help for a current problem without starting a program?

    Yes. Describe the current concern in the form. We review the property and explain whether targeted treatment, follow-up visits, a recurring program, or a different next step makes sense. Scope and pricing are discussed before you approve service.

    How does this relate to your Tree & Shrub Care program?

    This page helps you request care for an ornamental pest, disease, or decline concern. Our separate Tree & Shrub Care program provides six scheduled visits across the year for seasonal monitoring and appropriate plant-health care. We can discuss that option if ongoing support fits your landscape.

    How is ornamental treatment priced?

    Pricing depends on the number, size, type, and accessibility of the plants, the problem being addressed, and the recommended follow-up. We confirm the service scope and price before you approve. A request through this page does not book an application.

    Should I tell you about recent watering or treatments?

    Yes. Tell us when symptoms started and share recent planting, irrigation, pruning, weather, fertilizer, or pesticide changes. Include product names and application dates if you know them. This history helps us evaluate the concern and plan appropriate care.

    When can children and pets return after an application?

    Keep people and pets away from the treatment area during application. Follow the re-entry directions provided for the specific products used. The waiting period can vary by treatment.

    Do you prune, remove, or assess dangerous trees?

    Pruning, removal, stump work, and structural tree-risk assessment are outside this ornamental treatment service. A dead, storm-damaged, leaning, or otherwise unsafe tree should be evaluated by an appropriately qualified tree professional.

structured.hero_sub: Spotted leaves, sticky foliage, or a shrub that keeps declining? Grow Green looks at the plant, the symptoms, and the growing conditions to recommend treatment or the right next step.
structured.local_title: What are your plants telling you?
structured.local_lead: A few clear photos and a short history help us understand what is happening around the affected plants.

features.title: Sticky leaves & black coating
features.body: Honeydew from insects such as aphids, soft scales, or whiteflies can support sooty mold. We look for the source of the sticky residue.

features.title: Speckled or bronzed foliage
features.body: Tiny pale specks, bronzing, or fine webbing can be clues to mite feeding. Leaf undersides and active pests help clarify the cause.

features.title: Holes or chewed leaves
features.body: Missing leaf tissue calls for a closer look at feeding activity and the damage pattern. The insect may be gone by the time damage is noticed.

features.title: Leaf spots or powdery growth
features.body: Spots, blotches, or a powdery coating can point to disease. Plant identity and the pattern of symptoms help determine the next step.

features.title: Yellowing or wilting
features.body: We consider watering, drainage, roots, and nutrition along with pests and disease. Yellow leaves alone do not identify the problem.

features.title: Branch dieback or overall decline
features.body: Tell us whether one branch, one plant, or several plants are affected. That pattern helps guide a closer review of the plant and its surroundings.

real_faqs.q: Which plants can you help with?
real_faqs.a: We review problems affecting eligible ornamental trees and shrubs, including plants such as azaleas, hollies, camellias, gardenias, and similar landscape plantings. Plant size, access, species, and the suspected problem help determine whether our service is appropriate.

real_faqs.q: Can you identify the problem from a photo?
real_faqs.a: Photos are a useful starting point. We may need to examine the plant and growing conditions in person, and some problems require a sample or laboratory testing. A photo of one damaged leaf may not reveal the full cause.

real_faqs.q: Is every yellow or brown plant a pest or disease problem?
real_faqs.a: No. Watering, drainage, root injury, planting depth, sunlight, weather, and nutrient issues can produce similar symptoms. We consider those conditions before recommending an insecticide, fungicide, or nutritional treatment.

real_faqs.q: Will damaged leaves turn healthy again after treatment?
real_faqs.a: Existing holes and dead leaf tissue do not repair themselves. Appropriate treatment may reduce further damage and help protect new growth. Recovery depends on the cause, remaining plant health, and growing conditions; severely declined plants may need another solution.

real_faqs.q: Can I request help for a current problem without starting a program?
real_faqs.a: Yes. Describe the current concern in the form. We review the property and explain whether targeted treatment, follow-up visits, a recurring program, or a different next step makes sense. Scope and pricing are discussed before you approve service.
